## Why one regression can lie

One investment equation for ten firms, one price–income elasticity for 49
states: a pooled regression makes three promises about its error. The
slopes are the same for every unit, so that what is left over is noise and
not a different line. The noise has the same variance everywhere, so that
General Motors' shocks are no wilder than Diamond Match's. And the noise has
no memory, so that this year's shock says nothing about next year's beyond
what the unit effect already says. Each promise can be broken, each break
has a test, and each test has a repair.

The repairs are not the same kind. A wrong slope is a bias, and only a
different estimator fixes it. Unequal variances and memory leave the slopes
consistent and make the standard errors wrong, in either direction
[@baltagi2021, pp. 109, 115], so the first repair is an honest standard
error, and the second, when the structure is known well enough, is an
estimator that reweights the data and recovers efficiency. This note takes
the three promises in turn and ends with the menu of standard errors.

## 1. The composite error and its memory

Write the error of a one-way panel regression as $u_{it} = \alpha_i +
\varepsilon_{it}$, where $\alpha_i$ is the **unit effect**, everything fixed
about unit *i* that the regression leaves out, and $\varepsilon_{it}$ is the
**remainder**, the shock of unit *i* in year *t* ([fixed and random
effects](theory-fixed-random.qmd)). Under random effects the covariance is
$\Omega = \sigma^2_\alpha (I_N \otimes J_T) + \sigma^2_\varepsilon I_{NT}$,
so two errors of the same unit are correlated by $\sigma^2_\alpha /
(\sigma^2_\alpha + \sigma^2_\varepsilon)$ whatever the gap between the years
[@baltagi2021, eq. 2.17, p. 24]. A unit effect is therefore "serial
correlation that does not die out over time", and any test for serial
correlation run on pooled residuals will find it [@croissant2019, p. 95].

Memory of the other kind decays. Let the remainder follow a first-order
autoregression, an **AR(1)**,

$$
\varepsilon_{it} = \rho\, \varepsilon_{i,t-1} + \eta_{it}, \qquad |\rho| < 1,
\quad \eta_{it} \sim \mathrm{IID}(0, \sigma^2_\eta),
$$

so that a shock to investment this year carries into the next few years and
fades [@baltagi2021, eq. 5.8, p. 115]. The covariance of a unit's errors is
then

$$
E(u_i u_i') = \sigma^2_\alpha J_T + \sigma^2_\varepsilon V_\rho, \qquad
V_\rho = \begin{pmatrix}
1 & \rho & \cdots & \rho^{T-1} \\
\rho & 1 & \cdots & \rho^{T-2} \\
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
\rho^{T-1} & \rho^{T-2} & \cdots & 1
\end{pmatrix},
$$

a constant floor from $\alpha_i$ plus a band that thins with the distance
between years [@baltagi2021, eq. 5.32, pp. 125–126]. The tests of section 4
are all ways of telling the floor from
the band. The limit of the band is a **unit root** in the error, $\rho = 1$,
a shock that never fades ([why unit roots
matter](../04-time/index.qmd#sec-ur-why)); that case is the boundary this
chapter hands to the dynamic models of chapter 06.

Two transformations of the chapter leave their own fingerprint, and the
tests have to know it. Taking each unit's data in deviation from its mean,
the **within** transformation, turns uncorrelated remainders into residuals
with correlation $-1/(T-1)$ between any two years; first differencing turns
them into residuals with correlation $-0.5$ between neighbours and zero
beyond [@croissant2019, pp. 101, 103; @wooldridge2010, secs. 10.5.4 and
10.6.3]. A test of "no serial correlation" on within residuals is therefore
a test against $-1/(T-1)$, not against zero.

## 2. Same slopes

**Chow's F** fits one regression to everyone and one to each unit and
compares residual sums of squares. With $N$ units, $K' = K + 1$
coefficients each, the restricted residual sum $e'e$ and the unrestricted
one $\sum_i e_i'e_i$,

$$
F = \frac{(e'e - \sum_i e_i'e_i)/(N-1)K'}{\sum_i e_i'e_i / N(T-K')}
  \;\sim\; F_{(N-1)K',\, N(T-K')}
$$

under $H_0: \beta_i = \beta$ for all *i* and spherical errors,
$u \sim N(0, \sigma^2 I_{NT})$ [@chow1960; @baltagi2021, eq. 4.8, p. 77].
Restricting the slopes only, with the within fit as the restricted model,
gives the same statistic on $(N-1)K$ and $N(T-K-1)$ degrees of freedom
[@croissant2019, sec. 8.2.3, p. 192]. Pooling across years instead of units
swaps the roles of *N* and *T*.

Spherical errors is the catch. Under a random unit effect the Chow F "is
not the right test to perform": transform the model by $\Omega^{-1/2}$
first, so that the errors become spherical, then run the Chow F on the
transformed data. That is the **Roy–Zellner** test, operational once
$\Omega$ is replaced by a consistent estimate [@roy1957; @zellner1962;
@baltagi2021, eqs. 4.9–4.14, pp. 77–79]. Baltagi's Monte Carlo on a two-way
model with poolable data found the plain Chow test rejecting the true null
with "a high frequency" whenever the variance components were not small,
and the Roy–Zellner test holding its size [@baltagi1981; @baltagi2021, p.
79]. On Grunfeld the two tests agree, 27.75 and 4.35 on F(27, 170), both
rejections [@baltagi2021, p. 80]; the point is the size, not the verdict.
And a rejection is a statement about bias, not about what to report:
"imposing the pooling restriction reduces the variance of the pooled
estimator but may introduce bias if these restrictions are false"
[@croissant2019, p. 186], which is why the chapter shows the spread of the
individual slopes beside the pooled one.

**Swamy's random coefficients** make the spread a parameter. Let each
unit's coefficient vector be a draw around a common mean,

$$
y_i = Z_i \beta_i + \varepsilon_i, \qquad
\beta_i = \beta + \eta_i, \quad \eta_i \sim (0, \Delta),
$$

so that the error of unit *i* becomes $\varepsilon_i + Z_i \eta_i$ with
covariance $\sigma^2_i I_T + Z_i \Delta Z_i'$: heteroskedastic across units
and correlated within them [@swamy1970; @croissant2019, sec. 8.2.2, p. 187].
Swamy's estimator of the spread subtracts the sampling noise of the
unit-by-unit OLS slopes from their empirical covariance,

$$
\hat\Delta = \frac{1}{N-1}
  \sum_i (\hat\beta_i - \bar\beta)(\hat\beta_i - \bar\beta)'
  - \frac{1}{N} \sum_i \hat\sigma^2_i (Z_i'Z_i)^{-1},
$$

and GLS with the implied covariance is the Swamy estimator of $\beta$
[@croissant2019, p. 188]. The subtraction can leave $\hat\Delta$ not
positive definite. The **mean-group** estimator, the plain average of the
unit slopes with the empirical covariance of the $\hat\beta_i$ as its
dispersion ([common correlated
effects](../02-cross-dependence/index.qmd#sec-cce)), is Swamy's with equal
weights, "always non-negative definite", and the two converge as *T* grows
[@croissant2019, p. 190]. `plm::pvcm(model = "random")` returns
$\hat\Delta$ in `$Delta`.

Swamy also gave a test of $\beta_i = \beta$: the weighted dispersion of the
unit slopes around the pooled estimator,

$$
\hat S = \sum_{i=1}^{N} (\hat\beta_i - \tilde\beta_{WFE})'
  \frac{X_i' M_\tau X_i}{\hat\sigma^2_i} (\hat\beta_i - \tilde\beta_{WFE}),
$$

which is $\chi^2_{k(N-1)}$ as $T \to \infty$ with *N* fixed; it was built
for panels "where N is small relative to T" [@swamy1970; @pesaran2015, eq.
28.78, pp. 737–738]. With 49 states and 29 years, or 10 firms and 20, the
fixed-*N* asymptotics are not the ones at hand. **Pesaran and Yamagata**
standardise the same dispersion so that it is normal as *N* and *T* both
grow,

$$
\hat\Delta = \sqrt N \, \frac{N^{-1}\hat S - k}{\sqrt{2k}}, \qquad
\tilde\Delta = \sqrt N \, \frac{N^{-1}\tilde S - k}{\sqrt{2k}},
$$

where $\tilde S$ replaces each $\hat\sigma^2_i$ by a variance computed from
the pooled fixed-effects residuals. Both tend to $N(0, 1)$ under the null,
$\hat\Delta$ if $\sqrt N / T \to 0$ and $\tilde\Delta$ under the weaker
$\sqrt N / T^2 \to 0$; under normal errors the mean-and-variance adjusted
versions are valid with no restriction on how *N* and *T* grow
[@pesaran2008; @pesaran2015, eq. 28.79, pp. 738–739]. The price is in the
assumptions: errors independent across units and years and homoskedastic
within a unit, regressors strictly exogenous [@pesaran2015, p. 739]. Every
other section of this note is about panels that break at least one, which
is why Blomquist and Westerlund's heteroskedasticity-and-autocorrelation
robust version exists [@blomquist2013]. Neither test is implemented in R;
Stata's `xthst` is the reference implementation [@bersvendsen2021], and the
chapter states this as a limitation. A Hausman-type contrast of the
fixed-effects and mean-group slopes is the other candidate, and it lacks
power in every direction when the slopes are random draws, which is exactly
Swamy's alternative [@pesaran2008; @baltagi2021, p. 101].

## 3. Same variance

Big units have big shocks. **Heteroskedasticity**, unequal error
variances, is the rule "where the cross-sectional units may be of varying
size", and it leaves the slopes consistent but not efficient while the
classical standard errors "will be biased" [@baltagi2021, p. 109]. In a
panel it can sit in either component: Mazodier and Trognon put it in the
unit effect, $\alpha_i \sim (0, w_i^2)$, which gives each unit its own
quasi-demeaning fraction $\theta_i$; the alternative puts it in the
remainder, $\varepsilon_{it} \sim (0, w_i^2)$; and "it is hard to claim
that it is in one component and not the other" [@baltagi2021, eqs. 5.1–5.7,
pp. 109–111].

The tests are the gap. Verbon's Lagrange multiplier test takes both
variances to be the same parametric function of time-invariant unit
characteristics $Z_i$ [@verbon1980; @baltagi2021, p. 113]. Lejeune's tests
let $\sigma^2_{\varepsilon,it}$ and $\sigma^2_{\alpha,i}$ be distinct
functions of exogenous variables and test homoskedasticity jointly with the
absence of unit effects, so that OLS is the restricted model, once for a
random and once for a fixed effect [@lejeune2006; @baltagi2021, pp.
113–114]. Neither has an R implementation, and no panel test of
homoskedasticity does; the chapter shows the fan of residual spread against
unit size and runs a cross-section test on the within-transformed data as a
substitute, labelled as one.

The repair that needs no test is **Arellano's** variance for the within
estimator. Stack each unit's $T$ within-transformed observations, allow any
$T \times T$ covariance $\Sigma_i$ inside a unit and none across units, and
estimate the middle of White's sandwich with the unit's own residual outer
product:

$$
\widehat{\mathrm{var}}(\hat\beta_W) = (\tilde X'\tilde X)^{-1}
  \Big[ \sum_{i=1}^{N} \tilde X_i' \tilde u_i \tilde u_i' \tilde X_i \Big]
  (\tilde X'\tilde X)^{-1}
$$

[@arellano1987; @white1980; @baltagi2021, eqs. 2.13–2.16, pp. 18–19]. It is
robust to heteroskedasticity and to serial correlation of any form within a
unit, and its asymptotics are $N \to \infty$ with *T* fixed [@baltagi2021,
p. 18]. The plain White estimator on the within fit, which allows only the
variances to differ, is inconsistent for fixed *T* [@baltagi2021, p. 19],
and it understates the problem on every panel in the chapter. When *T* is
large as well, consistency needs either a limit on the serial correlation
or $T/N \to 0$ [@pesaran2015, sec. 26.7, p. 655].

The repair that recovers efficiency is **feasible GLS** on the whole $T
\times T$ block. Assume $\Omega = I_N \otimes \Sigma_T$ with $\Sigma_T$
unrestricted but the same for every unit, estimate it from the
cross-section,

$$
\hat\Sigma_T = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \hat e_i \hat e_i',
$$

and run GLS with it: the general GLS of Wooldridge, also called the Parks
estimator, a variant of Zellner's SUR [@parks1967; @zellner1962;
@wooldridge2010, sec. 10.4.3; @croissant2019, sec. 5.2.1, pp. 127–128]. It
allows any within-unit heteroskedasticity and serial correlation, rules out
cross-sectional correlation, and needs $N \gg T$ because it estimates
$T(T+1)/2$ covariances from *N* residual vectors [@croissant2019, p. 128].
On a wide short panel it is cheap; on ten firms over twenty years it is 210
parameters from ten observations, and the chapter shows that fit only to
read it as unreliable. Driscoll and Kraay note that the shortage of degrees
of freedom makes the estimate near-singular and the standard errors
downward biased; Beck and Katz document the same small-sample bias in the
pooled time series it was first used on [@driscoll1998; @beck1995;
@croissant2019, p. 128]. On within-transformed data the same recipe is
Kiefer's fixed-effects GLS, with one period dropped because the demeaned
residual covariance has rank $T - 1$ [@kiefer1980; @croissant2019, sec.
5.2.1.2, p. 131]; on first differences it is first-difference GLS, the
better choice when the fixed-effects residuals are not stationary
[@croissant2019, p. 132]. `plm::pggls` fits all three, and the estimated
$\hat\Sigma_T$ in `$sigma` is itself a picture of the error: off-diagonals
that stay flat with distance are a unit effect, off-diagonals that shrink
with distance are an AR(1) [@croissant2019, p. 129].

Heteroskedasticity has one more consequence in this book: under it the
maximum-likelihood spatial estimators of chapter 03 are inconsistent, and
the GM fit is the one to keep ([spatial fixed
effects](../03-spatial/index.qmd#sec-sp-fe); [@lin2010; @pesaran2015, p.
807]).

## 4. No memory

Every test here has to decide what to do about the unit effect, and the
answer sorts them into three kinds: joint tests of both departures at once,
marginal tests of one that assume the other away, and conditional tests of
one that allow the other at any size [@croissant2019, sec. 4.3.2, pp.
96–97]. A marginal test for serial correlation that assumes no unit effect
will reject because of the unit effect; a joint test rejects for either
reason and does not say which.

**Baltagi and Li** derived the joint Lagrange multiplier test from pooled
OLS residuals $\hat u$. With
$A = \hat u'(I_N \otimes J_T)\hat u / \hat u'\hat u - 1$, the Breusch–Pagan
ingredient, and $B = \hat u'\hat u_{-1} / \hat u'\hat u$, the first-order
autocorrelation of the stacked residuals,

$$
LM_1 = \frac{NT^2}{2(T-1)(T-2)} \left[ A^2 - 4AB + 2TB^2 \right]
  \;\sim\; \chi^2_2
$$

under $H_0: \sigma^2_\alpha = 0,\ \rho = 0$, and the statistic is the same
whether the alternative is AR(1) or MA(1) [@baltagi1991; @baltagi1995;
@baltagi2021, eq. 5.36, pp. 125–126]. The $A^2$ term alone is the
Breusch–Pagan test, $LM_2 = \sqrt{NT/2(T-1)}\, A$ in Honda's one-sided form;
the $B^2$ term alone is the Breusch–Godfrey test on the stacked residuals,
$LM_3 = \sqrt{NT^2/(T-1)}\, B$, which assumes no unit effect [@baltagi2021,
p. 126]. The cross term $-4AB$ is why the joint test is needed when both
are suspected. And $LM_3$ is the one not to use: with a unit effect present
"one is very likely to reject the null hypothesis of $H_3$ even if the null
is true. This is because the $\mu_i$ are correlated for the same individual
across time, and this will contribute to rejecting the null of no serial
correlation" [@baltagi2021, p. 127]. On Grunfeld it is 143.5 against the
conditional value 10.3 [@baltagi2021, p. 129].

Two families fix the marginal tests. The conditional test $LM_4$ tests
$\rho = 0$ given $\sigma^2_\alpha > 0$, from the residuals of the
random-effects model estimated by maximum likelihood, and is again the same
for AR(1) and MA(1) [@baltagi1995; @baltagi2021, p. 127]; it is
`plm::pbltest`, and it is the optimal test when a random effect is taken
for granted [@croissant2019, p. 97]. **Bera, Sosa-Escudero and Yoon** keep
the OLS residuals and correct each marginal statistic for its asymptotic
correlation with the other score,

$$
LM^*_\alpha = \frac{NT\,(2B - A)^2}{2(T-1)(1 - 2/T)}, \qquad
LM^*_\rho = \frac{NT^2\,[B - A/T]^2}{(T-1)(1 - 2/T)},
$$

each $\chi^2_1$ under its null and robust to a small amount of the other
departure; the four pieces add up, $LM^*_\alpha + LM_\rho = LM^*_\rho +
LM_\alpha = LM_1$, so the joint statistic decomposes into an adjusted test
of one direction plus the unadjusted test of the other [@bera2001;
@baltagi2021, p. 128]. These are `plm::pbsytest` with `test = "re"`,
`"ar"` and `"j"`, and Stata's `xttest1` prints the whole family: on
Grunfeld, 798.16 and 28.25 for the unit effect, 664.95 and 25.79 adjusted;
143.52 for serial correlation unadjusted and 10.31 adjusted; 808.47 joint
[@baltagi2021, Table 5.3, p. 129]. All of them assume normal, homoskedastic
errors [@croissant2019, p. 97].

The fixed-effects test uses within residuals $\tilde\varepsilon_{it}$,
whose unit effect is gone:

$$
LM_5 = \sqrt{\frac{NT^2}{T-1}} \;
  \frac{\tilde\varepsilon' \tilde\varepsilon_{-1}}
       {\tilde\varepsilon' \tilde\varepsilon}
  \;\sim\; N(0, 1)
$$

one-sided, for large *T* [@baltagi1995; @baltagi2021, eq. 5.43, p. 130]. It
differs from $LM_3$ only in the residuals, and "since the Within
transformation wipes out the individual effects whether fixed or random,
one can also use (5.43) to test for serial correlation in the random
effects models" [@baltagi2021, p. 130]. Nothing in plm is literally this
statistic; `plm::pbgtest` on a within fit is its Breusch–Godfrey cousin,
and the induced $-1/(T-1)$ of section 1 biases both toward rejection when
*T* is short [@croissant2019, p. 101]. The **Bhargava, Franzini and
Narendranathan** Durbin–Watson is the same residuals in Durbin–Watson form,

$$
d_p = \frac{\sum_i \sum_{t=2}^{T}
             (\tilde\varepsilon_{it} - \tilde\varepsilon_{i,t-1})^2}
           {\sum_i \sum_{t=1}^{T} \tilde\varepsilon_{it}^2},
$$

locally most powerful invariant near $\rho = 0$, with tabulated bounds for
balanced panels and, for very large *N*, the rule of simply asking whether
$d_p < 2$ [@bhargava1982; @baltagi2021, eq. 5.44, p. 130]. Baltagi and Wu's
locally best invariant statistic extends it to unequally spaced panels
[@baltagi1999; @baltagi2021, p. 121]; `plm::pbnftest` returns both without a
p-value, as Stata does [@baltagi2021, p. 130]. Inoue and Solon's portmanteau
test of all $(T-1)(T-2)/2$ autocorrelations at once needs $N \gg T^2/2$ and
is not run here [@inoue2006; @baltagi2021, p. 131].

**Wooldridge's** tests need no normality. The unobserved-effects test
averages the off-diagonal products of a unit's pooled residuals, scales by
their standard deviation, and is $N(0, 1)$ as *N* grows under any error
distribution; it has power against a unit effect and against serial
correlation alike, "trading some power against more specific alternatives
in exchange for robustness", and a rejection "should not be interpreted as
implying that the random effects error structure must be true"
[@wooldridge2010, sec. 10.4.4; @croissant2019, sec. 4.3.1, pp. 95–96]. The
within-based test regresses within residuals on their lag,

$$
\tilde\varepsilon_{it} = \phi\, \tilde\varepsilon_{i,t-1} + \xi_{it},
\qquad H_0: \phi = -\tfrac{1}{T-1},
$$

with a cluster-robust covariance, so it is valid for short *T* and large
*N* [@wooldridge2010, sec. 10.5.4; @croissant2019, sec. 4.3.5.1, p. 102].
The first-difference test regresses differenced residuals on their lag and
tests $\phi = -0.5$, the value uncorrelated original errors imply; Drukker's
Monte Carlo documents its size and power [@drukker2003; @wooldridge2010,
sec. 10.6.3; @croissant2019, p. 103]. Run both ways, `h0 = "fe"` and
`h0 = "fd"`, it is a choice of estimator: if the original errors are white
noise, within is efficient and the differenced errors show $-0.5$; if the
original errors are a random walk, the differenced errors are white noise
and first differences are efficient [@wooldridge2010, sec. 10.6.1;
@baltagi2021, pp. 22–23; @croissant2019, p. 103]. "Not rejecting one of the
two is evidence in favor of using the estimator corresponding to h0"; when
both reject, "the truth clearly lies in the middle" and "whichever
estimator is chosen will have serially correlated errors", which is the
case for robust standard errors [@croissant2019, p. 104].

## 5. The sandwich and its building blocks

Every robust covariance in the chapter is one formula. For a regression
with regressors $X$ and residuals $\hat u$, the variance of the OLS slopes
with a general error covariance is $(X'X)^{-1} (X'\Omega X) (X'X)^{-1}$,
and **White**'s insight is that the middle, the **meat**, needs only
$K(K+1)/2$ consistent numbers, not the $NT(NT+1)/2$ in $\Omega$
[@white1980; @croissant2019, sec. 5.1.1, p. 110]. The panel estimators
differ only in which residual products they let into the meat
[@millo2017]:

$$
\begin{aligned}
V_{wh} &= (X'X)^{-1}
  \Big[ \sum_i \sum_t \hat u_{it}^2\, x_{it} x_{it}' \Big] (X'X)^{-1}, \\
V_{cx} &= (X'X)^{-1}
  \Big[ \sum_{i=1}^{N} X_i' \hat u_i \hat u_i' X_i \Big] (X'X)^{-1}, \\
V_{ct} &= (X'X)^{-1}
  \Big[ \sum_{t=1}^{T} X_t' \hat u_t \hat u_t' X_t \Big] (X'X)^{-1}.
\end{aligned}
$$

$V_{wh}$ allows the variances to differ and nothing else [@croissant2019,
eq. 5.4, p. 111]. $V_{cx}$ **clusters by unit**: it allows any
heteroskedasticity and any serial correlation inside a unit, assumes units
independent, and is Arellano's estimator of section 3, Liang and Zeger's in
the statistics literature; its asymptotics are in *N*, the number of
clusters [@arellano1987; @liang1986; @croissant2019, eq. 5.2, p. 111].
$V_{ct}$ **clusters by year**: any cross-sectional correlation inside a
year, years independent, asymptotics in *T* [@croissant2019, eq. 5.5, p.
111]. "As a general rule, the estimator is asymptotic in the number of
clusters" [@croissant2019, p. 110]: ten firms are ten clusters, and the
Arellano standard errors on Grunfeld are noisy for that reason.

**Double clustering** adds the two and subtracts the diagonal that both
counted,

$$
V_{cxt} = V_{cx} + V_{ct} - V_{wh},
$$

robust to any dependence within a unit and within a year at once, with the
smaller of the two cluster counts having to grow [@cameron2011;
@thompson2011; @petersen2009; @croissant2019, eq. 5.6, p. 115]. It rules out
correlation between different units in different years. The kernel
estimators let that in, with weights that fall with the lag. Panel
**Newey–West** adds to $V_{wh}$ the lagged products of each unit's own
residuals,

$$
V_{nw,L} = V_{wh} + \sum_{l=1}^{L} w_l \big[ V_{wh,l} + V_{wh,l}' \big],
$$

with Bartlett weights $w_l = 1 - l/(L+1)$ and $L$ of the order of
$T^{1/4}$ [@newey1987; @croissant2019, eq. 5.10, pp. 110, 116, 119].
**Driscoll–Kraay** does the same to the year-clustered estimator,

$$
V_{scc,L} = V_{ct} + \sum_{l=1}^{L} w_l \big[ V_{ct,l} + V_{ct,l}' \big],
$$

so that cross-sectional correlation within a year and cross-serial
correlation between any two units up to $L$ years apart are both covered
[@driscoll1998; @croissant2019, eq. 5.11, p. 116]. Its price is the one the
spatial chapter already met: Driscoll and Kraay's conditions deliver
standard errors "robust to general forms of spatial and temporal dependence
as $T \to \infty$. However, if T is small, they conclude that the problem of
consistent nonparametric covariance matrix estimation is much less
tractable" [@baltagi2021, p. 394]; the practical minimum from their Monte
Carlo is $T > 20$–$25$, and *N* can grow at any rate [@croissant2019, p.
116]. Seventeen and twenty years sit at that floor. Beck and Katz's
**panel-corrected standard errors** take a different route to the same
dependence: assume the $N \times N$ cross-sectional covariance is the same
in every year, estimate it as $\sum_t \hat u_t \hat u_t' / T$, and plug it
into the sandwich; robust to cross-sectional heteroskedasticity and
correlation, and only to them [@beck1995; @croissant2019, eq. 5.13, p. 122].

Millo's comprehensive formula holds all of these,

$$
V_{cxt,L} = V_{ct} + \sum_{l=1}^{L} w_l [V_{ct,l} + V_{ct,l}']
  + V_{cx} - V_{wh} - \sum_{l=1}^{L} w_l [V_{wh,l} + V_{wh,l}'],
$$

and each named estimator is a choice of which terms to keep and which
weights to use: $L = 0$ gives double clustering, dropping $V_{cx} - V_{wh}$
and its lags gives Driscoll–Kraay, $w_l = 1$ gives Thompson's double
clustering with persistent shocks [@millo2017; @croissant2019, eq. 5.12 and
Table 5.1, p. 117]. `plm::vcovG` builds one block, `vcovHC`, `vcovSCC`,
`vcovNW` and `vcovDC` are the named sums, and the chapter's `se_table()`
lays the nine out side by side after every call has been shown. The blocks
are additive, so the table reads as a diagnosis: the gap between $V_{wh}$
and $V_{cx}$ is serial correlation within a unit, the gap between $V_{cx}$
and $V_{cxt}$ is what clustering by year adds, and a kernel estimator that
comes out *below* the clustered one is not reassurance but bias, because
the kernel "unduly downweighs the covariance between faraway observations"
when the dependence is a persistent unit effect [@petersen2009;
@croissant2019, pp. 119–121].

Two cautions on transformed data. The within transformation induces the
$-1/(T-1)$ correlation of section 1, so clustering by unit with unit
effects is right, clustering by year with time effects is right, and "the
combination of group clustering with time fixed effects and the reverse is
inappropriate" [@croissant2019, p. 121]. And a persistent unit effect left
in the residuals biases every kernel estimator, which is one reason to
demean or difference before applying one [@croissant2019, p. 121].

## If / then

| If | Then |
|---|---|
| Chow's F rejects but the errors have a unit effect | The plain F over-rejects; read the Roy–Zellner F on the GLS-transformed data [@baltagi2021, p. 79] |
| The slopes differ and *N* is large against *T* | Swamy's $\chi^2$ needs $T \to \infty$ at fixed *N*; the Δ tests are the right ones and are not in R [@pesaran2015, pp. 737–739] |
| $\hat\Delta$ is not positive definite | Report the mean-group dispersion, which always is [@croissant2019, p. 190] |
| Residual spread grows with unit size | Slopes stay consistent; replace the classical errors by Arellano's, or reweight by FGLS if $N \gg T$ [@baltagi2021, pp. 18–19, 109; @croissant2019, p. 128] |
| Only the unit effect is in doubt | Breusch–Pagan or Honda; $LM_3$ never, since the unit effect makes it reject [@baltagi2021, p. 127] |
| Both departures are suspected | The joint $LM_1$, then the BSY adjusted pair to say which [@baltagi2021, p. 128] |
| A random effect is taken as given | The conditional $LM_4$ from the ML fit [@croissant2019, p. 97] |
| The model is fixed effects | Within residuals: $LM_5$, BFN's $d_p$, or Wooldridge's within test against $-1/(T-1)$ [@baltagi2021, p. 130; @croissant2019, p. 102] |
| `h0 = "fe"` rejects and `h0 = "fd"` does not | First differences; the original errors look like a random walk [@croissant2019, pp. 103–104] |
| Both legs of the FD test reject | Either estimator with a serial-correlation-robust covariance [@croissant2019, p. 104] |
| Dependence is within units only | Cluster by unit; asymptotics in *N* [@croissant2019, p. 111] |
| Dependence is within years and within units | Double clustering; both counts must be large [@croissant2019, p. 115] |
| Units are correlated across years too, and $T > 20$–$25$ | Driscoll–Kraay [@croissant2019, p. 116; @baltagi2021, p. 394] |
| A kernel estimator is smaller than the clustered one | The unit effect is persistent and the kernel is biased; trust the cluster [@croissant2019, p. 121] |

## Open

- **Pesaran–Yamagata Δ** and its HAC extension have no R implementation;
  Stata's `xthst` is the benchmark, and the chapter defers it
  [@bersvendsen2021; @blomquist2013].
- **Verbon's and Lejeune's tests** of homoskedasticity, and the joint LM
  test of Baltagi, Bresson and Pirotte that nests them, are not
  implemented; the chapter has a picture and a substitute, not a test with
  a published size [@baltagi2021, pp. 113–114].
- **$LM_5$** is not literally in plm; `pbnftest` and `pbgtest` on within
  residuals are the nearest [@baltagi2021, p. 130].
- **Bester, Conley and Hansen's** group-membership HAC estimator is not
  implemented; its validity "relies on the capacity of the researcher to
  construct groups whose averages are approximately uncorrelated", and
  `plm::cortab` checks that precondition and nothing more [@pesaran2015, p.
  814].
- **Inoue–Solon** needs $N \gg T^2/2$ and is not run on any panel here
  [@baltagi2021, p. 131].

## Next

When the errors are nearer a random walk than white noise, the regression
itself is the problem, not its standard errors, and the lagged outcome
belongs on the right-hand side: [dynamic panel
GMM](../06-dynamic/theory-dynamic-gmm.qmd). The unit effect that every test
here had to allow for is the subject of [fixed and random
effects](theory-fixed-random.qmd).
